title: Psalm 79: Jerusalem in Rubble
summary: The nations have invaded God's inheritance, defiled his temple, and left Jerusalem in ruins, with the dead lying unburied. The people ask how long God will be angry and plead with him to pour out his wrath on the nations instead, to forgive their sins for the sake of his name, and to hear the groans of the captives. They promise to thank him forever as the sheep of his pasture.
story: Psalm 79 is the companion to Psalm 74. Both lament the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple, both ask how long God's anger will last, and both call Israel the sheep of God's pasture (74:1; 79:13). Where Psalm 74 dwells on the ruined sanctuary and appeals to God's power as creator, Psalm 79 focuses on the slaughter of the people, the unburied dead, and the need for forgiveness. It stands alongside Lamentations as one of Israel's responses to the catastrophe of exile, and it is followed by Psalm 80, another communal plea for restoration.
historical:
The heading reads “A Psalm of Asaph.” For Asaph and the Levitical guild of singers that bore his name, see Psalm 73. The psalm describes the defiling of the temple, the ruin of Jerusalem, and a massacre of its people. Most scholars connect it with the Babylonian conquest of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, described in 2 Kings 25 and Lamentations, and date it to the exile or shortly after. Verses 6 and 7 are nearly identical to Jeremiah 10:25, suggesting that one draws on the other or both on a common prayer, which fits that period.

A minority of interpreters have proposed the time of the Seleucid king Antiochus IV in the second century BC, when the temple was defiled. The book of 1 Maccabees, a Jewish history of that period, applies verses 2 and 3 to a massacre of faithful Jews in its own day, which shows the psalm was being read in that context. But most scholars think that application shows the psalm's later use rather than its origin, since the description of Jerusalem reduced to rubble fits the Babylonian destruction.
cultural:
In the ancient world, burial was a sacred duty, and leaving the dead unburied was one of the worst possible disgraces. Bodies left for birds and wild animals (verse 2) were a sign of total defeat and of a curse; the covenant curses in Deuteronomy 28:26 warned of exactly this fate. The absence of anyone to bury the dead (verse 3) means the population had been killed or taken captive.

The nations' mocking question, Where is their God? (verse 10), reflects the common belief that a people's defeat proved their god's weakness. For Israel the humiliation was not only national but theological: God's name was being dishonored. Paying back sevenfold into the lap (verse 12) draws on the image of the fold of a garment used to carry grain or goods; to repay into someone's lap meant to give them full measure. Sevenfold means complete repayment. The captives and those condemned to death (verse 11) were the survivors taken into exile or awaiting execution.
literary: The psalm is a communal lament in four movements. Verses 1 to 4 describe the disaster in stark detail. Verses 5 to 7 ask How long and call for God's wrath to be turned on the nations. Verses 8 to 12 plead for forgiveness and deliverance, grounding the plea in God's name, which appears three times (verses 6, 9, 9). Verse 13 closes with a vow of praise. The psalm repeatedly contrasts Your inheritance, Your temple, Your servants, and Your saints with the nations who defile them, emphasizing that the disaster is an offense against God himself. The word reproach frames the psalm: Israel has become a reproach (verse 4), and the neighbors' reproach is to be repaid (verse 12).

outline.t: How long, O LORD? Pour out wrath on the nations
Forgive us for the sake of Your name
Hear the captives and repay the scoffers
The sheep of Your pasture will praise You

doctrines.note: Verse 9 asks God to atone for the people's sins for the sake of his name. The people know the disaster is connected to their sin and ask for a covering that only God can provide, grounded in his own honor rather than their merit.
The psalm asks God to judge the nations that do not acknowledge him and to avenge the blood of his servants. It trusts God, not the people, to carry out vengeance.
The psalm gives voice to communal grief over massacre, desecration, and humiliation. It models bringing both sorrow and anger honestly to God.

words.note: Kipper, to atone, cover, or make reconciliation. It is the word used for the sacrifices of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). In verse 9 the people ask God himself to atone for their sins, with no temple left in which to offer sacrifice.
Nachalah, inheritance. In verse 1 Israel and its land are God's inheritance, his own possession. The invasion is therefore an assault on what belongs to God, which gives the psalm's plea its urgency.

Shem, name. God's name stands for his reputation and character. The people ask for help for the glory of Your name and for the sake of Your name (verse 9), appealing to God's honor rather than their own worth.

Chasid, a faithful or godly one, often translated saints. It is related to chesed, God's loyal love, and describes people who belong to him in covenant loyalty. In verse 2 their bodies lie unburied, a sharp picture of the cost of the disaster.

christ: Psalm 79 isn't quoted directly in the New Testament, but its cry echoes there. The souls of the martyrs in Revelation ask how long before God judges and avenges their blood (Revelation 6:10), taking up the plea of verses 5 and 10. The prayer that God would atone for sins for the sake of his name is answered in Christ, whom the New Testament presents as the atoning sacrifice for sins (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2), offered not because of human merit but out of God's own love. Jesus also mourned over Jerusalem and foresaw its destruction again (Luke 19:41-44), and the image of the people as sheep of God's pasture is fulfilled in Jesus, the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

hard.q: Is it right to pray for God's wrath and sevenfold repayment on other nations?
hard.a: The psalm asks God to pour out wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge him and to repay their reproach sevenfold. Readers rightly ask how that fits with Jesus' teaching to love enemies. Several points help. The prayer is spoken by a people who have just seen their city destroyed and their families slaughtered, and it hands vengeance to God instead of seeking it personally. Its concern is also God's honor: the nations have mocked God, and the people ask him to vindicate his name. The New Testament doesn't erase the longing for justice; the martyrs of Revelation 6:10 still ask God to avenge their blood. But in Christ, believers are also called to pray for their persecutors (Matthew 5:44), trusting God with both justice and mercy. Readers differ on how directly Christians should use such words today.

questions: The people ask for forgiveness for the sake of God's name, not their own merit. How does that shape the way you ask God for help?
The nations ask, “Where is their God?” When has suffering made you or others question God's presence?
How can you hold together grief over injustice, a longing for justice, and Jesus' call to pray for enemies?
